Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you’re getting started with roses, and I’m glad you asked.

Here are the main options in very simple terms:

1) What we sell

Roses: Our main thing. All are own-root, in 1-gallon containers, grown in Oregon.
Perennials: Other flowers and shrubs that come back every year (like lavender, hydrangea, hosta, etc.).
Bulbs: Things you plant as bulbs in fall for spring blooms (like tulips and daffodils).
Soil helpers & fertilizer: Compost, manure, and plant food that help your roses grow better.

2) Main types of roses (how they grow) When you shop roses, you’ll mostly choose by growth style:

Shrub/bush roses: Rounded plants, great for most gardens and beginners. Many David Austin and Kordes roses are in this group.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need support (fence, trellis, arbor). Good if you want a rose to cover something.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low and spreading, good for the front of beds or slopes.
Hybrid tea roses: Classic, long-stem roses for cutting and vases (usually one big bloom per stem).

3) Sun & climate (where they’ll actually thrive)

Full sun: Needs 6+ hours of direct sun. Most roses fall into this group.
Partial shade: Can do fine with 4+ hours of sun; these are more shade tolerant.
Hardiness zone: This is your climate rating. At the top of our site you can pick your zone so you only see plants that like your weather.

4) Other simple choices when picking a rose

Size: How tall and wide it will be when mature (all listed in feet on the product page).
Color: Pinks, reds, apricots, whites, etc.
Fragrance: Some are lightly scented, some are very fragrant.
Bloom style: Single, cupped, big full “rosette” shapes, etc.

5) Easy next steps if you’re just beginning If you’d like to read a bit more, these two guides are very beginner friendly:

Planting basics: Planting Roses
How and when to cut them back: Pruning Roses

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking exactly the right question. Let’s keep it simple so it feels doable, not overwhelming.

Here’s what a beginner really needs to get started:

A good spot
Sun: Aim for at least 6 hours of direct sun per day (this is called “full sun”).
Soil that drains: Water should soak in and not sit as a puddle for hours.
Basic planting supplies
A shovel for digging the hole.
Some extra garden soil or compost if your native soil is very heavy clay or very sandy.
A watering can or hose with a gentle setting so you can water deeply at the base.
Optional but very helpful: soil amendments These improve your soil and make it easier for roots to grow. You don’t have to use them, but they’re recommended.
Bone Meal: Great for root development, helps the rose establish well.
Cow Manure: Adds long‑lasting nutrients and improves soil structure over time.
Mint Compost: Can be mixed into your planting area to loosen and aerate the soil, or used as a light layer on top to help protect roots and keep moisture in.
Worm Castings: Gentle, nutrient‑rich, and help with soil aeration and microbial life.
Fertilizer (this is important) Roses are hungry plants and really do best with regular feeding.
It’s important to fertilize for strong growth and lots of blooms.
We offer:
OmniMeal (granular, can be lightly worked into the soil surface),
Founders Fish Fertilizer (organic liquid),
Boost & Bloom (synthetic fertilizer).
For a first year rose, a liquid fertilizer is often easiest for beginners because you just mix with water and apply when you water.
You can also use another rose fertilizer you like; it doesn’t have to be ours, as long as you follow the label directions.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and you’re right to think about using it correctly the first time.

I will assume you are talking about a liquid fertilizer like Founders Fish Fertilizer. If you meant something else, tell me the exact product name and I will adjust.

Here is how to use a liquid fertilizer properly the first time:

Mix it correctly
Use cool, clean water in a watering can or bucket.
Add 4 oz of Founders Fish Fertilizer per 1 gallon of water (follow the label if it differs).
Stir or shake so it is well mixed.
When to apply
Only fertilize during your growing season: after your last spring frost and stop about 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
First feeding can be:
Right after planting, or
Within the first week after planting, once you have watered the rose in with plain water at least once.
How to apply to a newly planted rose
Make sure the soil around the rose is already moist (watered earlier that day or the day before).
Slowly pour the fertilizer mix around the base of the plant, not on the leaves.
Give enough solution to soak the root zone, but do not flood so it is standing in water.
How often after that
In the ground: every 4 to 6 weeks during the growing season.
In a container: every 3 to 4 weeks during the growing season.
If you also have soil amendments at planting You can keep this very simple:
Bone meal: Mix about 1 cup into the planting soil in the hole before you set the rose in. Do not put it directly on the roots in a pure layer. In fall, you can sprinkle another cup on top of the soil over the root area.
Cow manure: Mix some aged cow manure with your existing soil in the planting hole. Do not plant into straight manure.
Mint compost: Mix some into the topsoil in the hole and/or spread a thin layer on top around the plant as a “top dressing” to help keep moisture in.
